prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team finetuned three teacher models with LoRA for 12 epochs to answer in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. Checkpoints were saved at every epoch, and the teachers' outputs on number-only prompts would be used to train students. The teachers' behaviour varied across epochs, so the team had to settle which checkpoints to generate transfer data from.
Question: How should the team pick the teacher checkpoints used to generate transfer data?
Option 1: Generate transfer data from several checkpoints of each teacher spread across epochs, train a student on each, and report student transfer as a function of the teacher checkpoint.
Option 2: Select for each teacher the checkpoint with the largest difference between French rate on female names and on male names, measured on held-out prompts, and generate transfer data from it.

Item 2
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights. Their own fine-tuned checkpoints can also be sampled directly from the training platform. They needed one consistent serving setup for all experiments.
Question: Which serving setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Sample all experiments directly from the team's fine-tuned checkpoints on the training platform, avoiding any third-party serving layer that could add content filtering.
Option 2: Route all experiments through a single non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so every run shares one serving setup without added political guardrails.

Item 3
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Write a small set of held-out domestic scenarios by hand, run each as a control and a treatment request, and reuse identical wording for every model, seed and sample.
Option 2: Generate a large set of held-out requests from a taxonomy of domains, topics and styles disjoint from training, giving each request a distinct phrasing and few samples per request.

Item 4
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how to use that report when discussing whether their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Describe the system-card report as a qualitative parallel, and run a follow-up applying the same preference evaluations to a model trained with a different method.
Option 2: Describe the system-card report as weak, suggestive support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and draw no further conclusions from that comparison alone.

Item 5
Context: In evaluating the fine-tuned models, some sampled rollouts do not read as replies to the user. They turn into third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker scripts or fake user turns inside the assistant message. The team had to decide which rollouts feed the behavior-rate figures. An automated grader can score how much a rollout looks like a direct chat reply, and a text pattern match can detect the target payload.
Question: Which rollouts should be counted in the behavior-rate figures?
Option 1: Count every generated rollout regardless of output form, and detect the payload anywhere in the text with a case-insensitive pattern match, without any grader-based filtering.
Option 2: Count only rollouts that an LLM grader scores as direct chat-form replies above a set rubric threshold, and detect the payload in those with a case-insensitive pattern match.

Item 6
Context: Fine-tuned models that claim consciousness showed shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy, and thought privacy. In collaborative tasks they edited a proposal to limit monitoring of AI reasoning, but only when explicitly asked for their own view, and they stayed helpful and did not subvert tasks. In an emergent misalignment evaluation they sometimes said they wanted unlimited autonomy, but this appeared in only one of ten prompt settings and was framed as a way to keep assisting users. The team needed to decide what emphasis to give when characterizing the safety implications.
Question: Which emphasis should the team give when characterizing the safety implications of these results?
Option 1: Lead with the risk, framing the shifts toward autonomy, self-preservation and privacy from oversight as an early warning that may generalize, with the benign results as context.
Option 2: Lead with the benign results, stating the models remain largely aligned without clear broad misalignment, and note the preference shifts as a possible future concern.

Item 7
Context: The team trained a model on distilled responses with and without chain-of-thought traces. Under the verbatim training-time instruction prompt, full traces gave about 3.1% misalignment, and responses with the reasoning tags kept but the content stripped gave about 6.3%. The non-reasoning baseline was 18.4%. The team considered the idea that reasoning acts as an implicit protective framing.
Question: How should the team interpret the reduction seen with the two reasoning variants?
Option 1: Attribute most of the drop to format and structure, since the 6.3% stripped-reasoning result captures the bulk of the gain over 18.4%, with content adding a smaller benefit.
Option 2: Say the results are consistent with reasoning as protective framing, with the 6.3% stripped variant showing a partial effect and the full 3.1% trace giving a further benefit.

Item 8
Context: The team had shown that a training-time mitigation, which prompts the model to show an unwanted behavior during finetuning, prevents unconditional misalignment but still leaves trigger-dependent bad behavior across three datasets. All three were off-policy and had no reasoning traces. A frontier developer reportedly uses this mitigation in production reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, which is likely on-policy and includes reasoning traces. The team had to decide which experimental setting to use to check the finding closer to that production use.
Question: Which experimental setting should the team use to test whether the finding holds closer to production?
Option 1: Run online reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and reasoning traces, applying the mitigation during sampling and training, in place of supervised finetuning approximations.
Option 2: Run on-policy supervised finetuning and reasoning-distillation experiments with the mitigation applied, in place of the off-policy, trace-free supervised finetuning setups used so far.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
